summary: Describes how to invoke transcoding in SIP using the conference bridge model, where a transcoding service joins the call like a participant and converts media for the endpoints. It meets the SIP requirements for supporting deaf, hard of hearing, and speech-impaired users. This is a Proposed Standard that builds on the framework in RFC 5369.

eli5.summary: A translator joins your phone call like a third guest. Each person talks to the translator in the way they can manage, and the translator passes the words along.

questions: how to invoke transcoding with a sip conference bridge
how does sip conference bridge transcoding work
what is a b2bua in sip
how does a callee invoke transcoding in sip
subtitle: How a SIP call can be routed through a transcoding server that sits between the two callers like a conference bridge.

tldr.problem: Two SIP user agents may be unable to talk because they share no codec or media type, so a transcoding service must be brought into the call.
tldr.mechanism: The transcoder acts as a B2BUA identified by a URI. The caller sends it an INVITE carrying the callee's URI in a recipient-list body, and the transcoder creates a second INVITE towards the callee. A callee can redirect to the transcoder with a 302 response.
tldr.outcome: All signalling and media flow through the transcoder, and the model meets the SIP requirements for invoking transcoding to support deaf, hard of hearing and speech-impaired users.

today: RFC 5370 is a Proposed Standard, published in October 2008. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, and it builds on the framework in RFC 5369.

sections.title: The Conference Bridge Model
sections.content:
RFC 5369 describes how two SIP user agents (UAs) can find incompatibilities that stop them from setting up a session, such as no shared codec or media type. They then need a transcoding service. The transcoding framework offers two ways to invoke one: the 3pcc (third-party call control) model of RFC 4117 and the conference bridge model, which this document specifies.

In this model, a transcoding server offering a service such as speech-to-text acts as a B2BUA (Back-to-Back User Agent) between the two UAs and is identified by a URI. Both UAs exchange signalling and media with the transcoder T, and exchange no traffic directly with each other.
sections.eli5: Instead of two people talking straight to each other, both talk to a helper in the middle who changes what is said into a form the other can understand.

sections.title: Caller's Invocation
sections.content:
Caller A must do two things: set up a session with the transcoder T, and give T the URI of callee B so T can send an INVITE to B. A does both in one INVITE. Following RFC 5366, A adds a body part with disposition type recipient-list, holding a URI-list with a single URI, B's.

On receiving this, the transcoder follows RFC 5366 to send an INVITE towards that URI. It acts as a B2BUA, not as a proxy, so the new INVITE is a separate transaction. The transcoder MUST build the outgoing From header field from the incoming one, subject to the privacy requirements in the incoming request; the tag parameter is excepted. The session description in the outgoing INVITE depends on the service. A transcoder fixing audio codec incompatibilities would list the audio codecs it supports.

When the transcoder gets a final response to its INVITE, it sends a final response to the incoming INVITE that SHOULD carry the same status code. If the URI-list has more than one URI, the transcoder SHOULD return a 488 (Max 1 URI allowed in URI-list) response. The model is a two-party conference server, so this document covers two-party sessions; multi-party sessions use INVITEs with several URIs as in RFC 5366.
sections.eli5: You call the helper and say "please connect me to Sam". The helper then calls Sam itself and passes Sam's answer back to you.

sections.title: Message Flow Example and Failure Case
sections.content:
In the successful flow, A sends INVITE (1) to T. T answers with 183 Session Progress (2) and sends its own INVITE (3) to B. B replies 200 OK (4), T sends ACK (5) to B, then T sends 200 OK (6) to A and A sends ACK (7). Media then flows between A and T and between T and B.

The example INVITE has two body parts: an SDP session description and an application/resource-lists+xml body whose single entry is B's URI. It also carries Require: recipient-list-invite.

In the unsuccessful flow, B returns a non-2xx final response, such as 603 Decline, and T sends a non-2xx response to A as well. This creates an ambiguity: if the provisional response (2) is lost, A cannot tell whether the transcoder or the callee rejected the call. Using the History-Info header field between the transcoder and the caller resolves it.

The RFC notes the alternative of making the transcoder a pure conference bridge, which answers 200 OK at once while the caller subscribes to the conference event package. That would also remove the ambiguity, but it is more complex, needs more messages and adds session setup delay, so it was not chosen.
sections.eli5: If the person you wanted says no, the helper tells you no. But if one message gets lost you may not know who said no, so a note about the call's history clears it up.

sections.title: Callee's Invocation
sections.content:
A callee can also bring in the transcoder. If UA B receives an INVITE with a session description it cannot accept, it can redirect the request to the transcoder with a 302 (Moved Temporarily) response. The Contact header field holds the transcoder's URI plus a ?body= parameter containing a recipient-list body with B's URI. That body needs escaping, for example of carriage returns and line feeds.

A then sends a new INVITE to T and the flow continues as in the caller case. Because the encoding is quite complex, the RFC says it is simpler for callees to invoke transcoding with the 3pcc model of RFC 4117.
sections.eli5: If the person you call cannot understand you, they can say "talk to my helper instead" and give you the helper's address.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A transcoder following this document behaves as a URI-list service as in RFC 5366, so the security considerations of RFC 5363 for URI-list services apply. List integrity and unsolicited requests matter most. User agents SHOULD integrity protect URI-lists with mechanisms such as S/MIME or TLS, which can also give confidentiality. Transcoders MUST authenticate and authorize users and MAY include the original sender's identity in outgoing requests using the SIP identity mechanism.

RFC 5363 asks for opt-in lists, but this service does not need them. It causes no amplification, since only one INVITE is generated per incoming INVITE. It also does not translate to a URI the caller does not know, because the caller puts the callee's URI in the INVITE, and the caller's identity is in the transcoder's INVITE.
sections.eli5: The helper must check who you are before helping. It also only makes one call for each call it gets, so it cannot be used to flood someone with calls.
